blocks.content: Imagine an API server as a single cashier at a supermarket. On a normal day it handles the queue just fine. Then a huge sporting event ends and everyone orders food delivery at the exact same moment, the queue explodes, the cashier crashes, and everyone gets an error.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785274111594-661076986.png
blocks.alt: The same total demand, handled by one overwhelmed cashier versus several cashiers with someone directing the queue

blocks.content: A load balancer solves this by sitting in front of multiple servers and distributing incoming requests across them. No single server gets overwhelmed, and if one goes down entirely, the others simply keep serving, users never notice at all. This topic covers what a load balancer actually does, the difference between working at the transport layer versus the application layer, health checks, the sticky session problem, the real categories of load balancers in use today, and where they actually fit into a real architecture.
1. What a Load Balancer Actually Does
blocks.text: 1. What a Load Balancer Actually Does

blocks.content: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785274113636-834872963.png
blocks.alt: Three responsibilities, working together continuously, not just a one-time routing decision

blocks.content: A load balancer distributes incoming traffic across every currently healthy server based on a chosen algorithm, continuously health checks each one, and automatically stops sending traffic to anything that fails a check, resuming once it recovers.

A load balancer acts like a traffic cop for servers, it distributes incoming requests across multiple servers, checks their health, and redirects traffic away from failed or overloaded servers automatically.

blocks.title: The Difference in Concrete Numbers
blocks.text: A single server that can handle 200 requests per second receiving 1000 requests per second fails 800 of them outright. The exact same 1000 requests per second, spread across five identical servers by a load balancer, becomes 200 each, a load every one of them can handle comfortably. If one of those five servers fails, the load balancer simply stops sending it traffic, users never notice a thing.

blocks.content: 2. A Quick Word on Algorithms

The algorithm decides exactly which server gets the next request, round robin, weighted round robin, least connections, IP hash, least response time, and random are all real, commonly used approaches, each fitting a different situation. This topic focuses on what a load balancer is and does more broadly, the dedicated Load Balancing Algorithms topic covers each of these in real depth, with worked examples for when each one is genuinely the right choice.
3. Layer 4 vs Layer 7 Load Balancing
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785274115446-991003812.png
blocks.alt: How much of the request a load balancer is willing to inspect before routing it determines both its speed and its intelligence

blocks.content: Layer 4 load balancing works on raw TCP or UDP, routing purely by IP address and port, never looking inside the request itself, making it extremely fast since there is nothing to parse. AWS Network Load Balancer and HAProxy in its simplest mode are real examples.

Layer 7 load balancing works on HTTP or HTTPS directly, reading the full request, URL, headers, cookies, even the body, letting it route based on actual content rather than just address and port. It is slower than Layer 4 but considerably more flexible and intelligent. AWS Application Load Balancer, Nginx, and Envoy are all real Layer 7 implementations.

Neither layer is universally better, Layer 4's speed makes it the right choice when raw throughput matters most and routing decisions genuinely do not need to look at request content, while Layer 7's visibility into the request is exactly what makes path-based and host-based routing possible in the first place.
4. Layer 7 Routing: Path-Based and Host-Based
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785274117080-22638938.png
blocks.alt: Because a Layer 7 load balancer can read the full request, it can split one domain across many independent backend services

blocks.content: Because it sees the full request, a Layer 7 load balancer can route different URL paths to entirely different backend services, exactly how API gateways work in a microservices architecture. Requests to /api/users go to the user service, /api/orders to the order service, /api/payments to the payment service, all under one single public domain.

This is a direct application of the same reverse proxy routing idea covered in the earlier Proxy vs Reverse Proxy topic, a load balancer performing path-based routing is, functionally, doing exactly what a reverse proxy does, since both roles frequently live in the very same piece of software.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785274118675-865825671.png
blocks.alt: Routing by the request's own host header lets several services live behind entirely separate domains instead

blocks.content: Host-based routing works similarly but decides based on the domain itself, the host header, rather than the URL path, useful when separate services are meant to be exposed through their own distinct domains rather than one shared one.

Choosing between the two is largely a product and branding decision as much as a technical one, path-based routing keeps everything under one domain, simpler for clients, while host-based routing lets each service carry its own independent, memorable subdomain.

blocks.title: A Real Nginx Configuration, Explained
blocks.content: An nginx config defining separate upstream pools for a user service, an order service, and a payment service, then matching incoming request paths against location blocks for /api/users, /api/orders, and /api/payments, is exactly this pattern in practice: client connects to nginx, nginx inspects the URL, matches it against a location block, and forwards to the correct upstream pool, with the response returned back through the same path.
5. Health Checks
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785274120298-798367390.png
blocks.alt: Health checks range from a simple connection attempt to genuinely confirming every dependency the application itself relies on

blocks.content: A load balancer constantly checks whether each backend server is genuinely alive. A TCP health check simply attempts a connection to the server's port, fastest of the three, but only confirms the port is open, not that the actual application behind it is working correctly. An HTTP health check sends a real request, commonly to a dedicated /health endpoint, and expects a 200 response, confirming the application itself is genuinely responding. A deep health check goes further still, verifying the server's own critical dependencies, its database connection, its cache, even disk space, catching a degraded state before it becomes a full outage.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396019238-297305812.png
blocks.alt: A failed check removes a server from rotation immediately, and a later passing check brings it right back in, entirely automatically

blocks.content: If a server fails a health check, the load balancer stops sending it traffic immediately. When it recovers and starts passing checks again, it is added back into rotation automatically, with no manual intervention needed at all.

Choosing how aggressively to check matters too, checking too infrequently means a genuinely failed server keeps receiving real user traffic for longer than necessary, while checking too aggressively adds its own constant background load to every single server, purely to answer health probes rather than genuine user requests.
6. Sticky Sessions
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785274123551-168300704.png
blocks.alt: A user's session data stored only in one server's own memory becomes invisible the moment a different server handles their next request

blocks.content: By default, any request can go to any server. But if a user's session is stored in one specific server's own memory, rather than somewhere shared, that user needs to keep hitting that exact same server, otherwise their session appears to simply vanish, and they get logged out or unauthorized unexpectedly.

Sticky sessions are really a symptom of a stateful backend, session data tied to one specific server instance. This is exactly what breaks clean load balancing, since requests for that one user must keep returning to the same instance.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785274125080-667399499.png
blocks.alt: Moving session data into a shared store removes the constraint entirely, letting any server legitimately handle any request

blocks.content: The real fix is moving session data out of individual servers entirely, into a shared store like Redis that every server can read from. Once that is done, genuinely any server can handle any request, restoring full, unconstrained load balancing and clean failover, sticky session configuration becomes unnecessary.

An increasingly common alternative avoids a shared store entirely, encoding session data directly into a signed token, a JWT, that the client itself carries on every request. Any server can then verify and read that token without needing to look anything up anywhere at all, genuinely stateless in the fullest sense.

The example below simulates exactly the health-check-driven behavior described earlier: a pool of servers where one is deliberately marked unhealthy partway through, correctly skipped by every subsequent round robin assignment, and then correctly included again the moment it is marked healthy once more.
7. Types of Load Balancers
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785274126719-567278512.png
blocks.alt: Four broad categories, differing mainly in where they run and how much you manage yourself

blocks.content: {"headers":["Type","Examples","Notes"],"rows":[["Hardware","F5 BIG-IP, Citrix ADC","Dedicated physical appliances, high performance, high cost"],["Software","Nginx, HAProxy, Envoy","Runs on ordinary servers, flexible and widely used"],["Cloud managed","AWS Application Load Balancer, AWS Network Load Balancer, Google Cloud Load Balancing","Fully managed by the cloud provider, scales automatically"],["DNS based","Amazon Route 53, Cloudflare","Distributes traffic by returning different IPs to different clients"]]}

Hardware load balancers were once the default choice for large enterprises, offering strong, predictable performance but requiring real physical installation and meaningful upfront cost. Software load balancers shifted that same capability onto ordinary commodity servers, trading a little raw performance for enormous flexibility and far lower cost, which is exactly why they became the dominant choice for most modern systems.

Cloud managed load balancers remove infrastructure management entirely, the provider handles scaling, patching, and redundancy on your behalf, at the cost of being tied to that specific cloud provider's own ecosystem. DNS based load balancing, covered in depth in its own dedicated topic later in this module, works differently still, distributing load by literally answering the same domain name lookup with different IP addresses to different clients.
8. Load Balancers in a Real Architecture
blocks.text: 8. Load Balancers in a Real Architecture

blocks.content: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785274128626-727573455.png
blocks.alt: Large systems commonly layer load balancers, one global entry point routing to independently scaled subsystems below it

blocks.content: In a system design interview, the moment a design has more than one server, a load balancer belongs in front of them. Larger systems commonly use several layers of load balancing at once. A global Layer 7 load balancer serves as the system's entry point, inspecting the request path and splitting traffic, requests starting with /api/ go to an API load balancer, which itself distributes traffic across multiple API servers, while requests starting with /static/ go to a separate static load balancer routing to CDN nodes serving images, CSS, and JavaScript.

One Layer 7 load balancer at the top intelligently routes traffic to different subsystems, API versus static content, and each subsystem then has its own load balancer scaling independently underneath it. This separation improves performance, scalability, and overall system organization all at once.
9. TLS Termination at the Load Balancer
blocks.text: 9. TLS Termination at the Load Balancer

blocks.content: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785274130234-997288207.png
blocks.alt: The load balancer holds the certificate and decrypts traffic, letting backend servers run plain HTTP internally

blocks.content: Just like a reverse proxy, a load balancer commonly holds the TLS certificate itself, decrypting incoming HTTPS traffic and forwarding plain HTTP to backend servers internally. This means exactly one certificate to manage and renew, and the CPU cost of encryption handled once, centrally, rather than repeated on every individual backend server.
This exact mechanism is covered in full depth in the TLS Handshake topic, the load balancer here simply plays the same server role that any TLS-terminating endpoint plays.
10. Connection Draining
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396019241-387037600.png
blocks.alt: A server being taken down finishes its existing in-flight work first, rather than abruptly cutting active users off mid-request

blocks.content: When a server needs to be taken out of rotation, for a deployment, a scale-down, or planned maintenance, abruptly cutting it off mid-request would break whatever that server was actively handling. Connection draining instead stops sending it any new requests immediately, while letting its existing in-flight requests finish naturally, only removing it from the pool entirely once those are done.

Without this, a rolling deployment across a fleet of servers would visibly interrupt some fraction of real user requests every single time, exactly the kind of avoidable disruption connection draining exists to prevent.
11. Rate Limiting at the Load Balancer
blocks.text: 11. Rate Limiting at the Load Balancer

blocks.content: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396024007-873657939.png
blocks.alt: Excess requests from one client are rejected right at the edge, before ever reaching a backend server at all

blocks.content: Many load balancers can enforce per-client rate limits directly, rejecting requests beyond an allowed threshold before they ever reach a backend server at all. This protects backend capacity from a single misbehaving or abusive client without that client's excess traffic ever costing the application layer anything.

Enforcing this right at the load balancer, rather than deeper inside application code, means a single misbehaving client is stopped before it ever spends a single CPU cycle of actual backend capacity at all.
12. A Brief Note on Global Load Balancing
blocks.text: 12. A Brief Note on Global Load Balancing

blocks.content: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785274135232-128521727.png
blocks.alt: Directing each request to its nearest regional deployment cuts latency and spreads load geographically

blocks.content: Everything covered so far load balances within a single location. Real global systems also load balance across entire regions, routing a request from anywhere in the world to whichever regional deployment is actually closest to it. This involves DNS-based routing and anycast, both covered in their own dedicated topics later in this module, alongside a direct comparison between global and regional load balancers specifically.

Everything this topic has covered so far still applies fully within each individual region, global load balancing simply adds one more layer deciding which region a request reaches in the first place.
13. A Common Mistake: Forgetting the Load Balancer Itself Needs Redundancy
blocks.text: 13. A Common Mistake: Forgetting the Load Balancer Itself Needs Redundancy

blocks.content: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785274137032-893125875.png
blocks.alt: A single load balancer instance is itself a single point of failure for every server sitting behind it

blocks.content: A load balancer solves the problem of any one backend server becoming a single point of failure, but a design that stops there quietly introduces a new one, the load balancer itself. If it runs as one single instance, its own failure takes down access to every healthy backend server behind it at once, regardless of how well distributed the actual traffic was.

This is a genuinely easy detail to overlook precisely because the load balancer is usually the component that FIXES availability problems elsewhere in a design, it is easy to forget it needs the exact same treatment applied to itself.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785274138731-532220876.png
blocks.alt: Running multiple load balancer instances removes the load balancer's own single point of failure the same way it removed the backend server's

blocks.title: The Fix Is the Same Idea, One Layer Up
blocks.content: Real production deployments run multiple load balancer instances, often behind DNS round robin or a cloud provider's own managed, inherently redundant load balancing service, applying the exact same redundancy principle to the load balancer that the load balancer itself applies to backend servers.

Most managed cloud load balancing services already handle this transparently, one genuine reason many teams choose a cloud managed option specifically over running and redundantly maintaining their own software load balancer instances entirely by hand.
Worked Example

A food delivery app's backend starts as a single server. As traffic grows, the team adds a Layer 7 load balancer in front of three identical API servers, using round robin since all three have equal capacity. They configure an HTTP health check against a dedicated /health endpoint, one that also confirms the database connection is genuinely alive, not just that the process itself is running.

They also enable connection draining for deployments, so pushing a new release no longer interrupts users mid-checkout, and run two load balancer instances behind a cloud provider's own managed service, specifically so the load balancer itself is never the single point of failure for the entire system.

Session data, previously stored in each server's own memory, is moved into a shared Redis instance specifically so any of the three servers can handle any request. When traffic later grows enough to need path-based routing for a newly split-out payments service, the same load balancer is extended to route /api/payments to its own separate, independently scaled pool, without touching how the existing user and order traffic is handled at all.
Common Mistakes

["Running a single load balancer instance with no redundancy of its own, quietly reintroducing the exact single point of failure the load balancer was meant to remove","Relying only on a TCP health check when an HTTP or deep health check would have caught a genuinely broken application dependency far earlier","Storing session data in individual server memory and reaching for sticky sessions instead of the more robust fix of a shared session store","Choosing Layer 4 for a scenario that genuinely needs path-based or host-based routing, when only Layer 7 can actually see enough of the request to make that decision"]
items: Running a single load balancer instance with no redundancy of its own, quietly reintroducing the exact single point of failure the load balancer was meant to remove
Relying only on a TCP health check when an HTTP or deep health check would have caught a genuinely broken application dependency far earlier
Storing session data in individual server memory and reaching for sticky sessions instead of the more robust fix of a shared session store
Choosing Layer 4 for a scenario that genuinely needs path-based or host-based routing, when only Layer 7 can actually see enough of the request to make that decision

blocks.content: Practice

Design a two-layer load balancing setup for a system with a public API and a separately hosted admin dashboard, both under the same parent domain, deciding whether path-based or host-based routing fits better, and justify the choice.

Then explain, in your own words, exactly what happens to an in-flight request if the specific server handling it fails a health check mid-request, versus what happens to a brand new request arriving right after that same failure.

Finally, list every place in a real production deployment where a single instance of something could quietly become a new single point of failure, the load balancer itself, the health check mechanism, and anything else you can identify.
Key Takeaway

A load balancer distributes incoming traffic across multiple servers, continuously health checks them, and automatically routes around anything unhealthy, turning a single fragile server into a resilient pool. Layer 4 load balancing is fast but blind to request content, Layer 7 is slower but can route by path or host, exactly what makes API gateways and microservices architectures possible. Sticky sessions are a sign of a stateful backend, best solved by moving session data into a shared store rather than pinning users to one server, and the load balancer itself needs the same redundancy it provides to everything behind it, since a single load balancer instance is just as much a single point of failure as a single backend server ever was.

Everything covered here, algorithms, health checks, TLS termination, connection draining, rate limiting, is a piece of the same underlying goal: making a pool of individually fallible servers behave, from the outside, like one reliable, always-available system.
